title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
description: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are
body: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak. Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added. The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain. DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said. The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate". Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing. Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

schema.headline: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak

title: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise
description: Tens of thousands of people have gathered in India's capital Delhi for a major opposition rally demanding the resignation of the country's chief elect
body: Tens of thousands of people have gathered in India's capital Delhi for a major opposition rally demanding the resignation of the country's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.The rally, organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, has brought together some of India's most prominent politicians at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi.They arrived at the venue on Sunday after travelling in jeeps through crowds of cheering supporters.Among those attending were Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, as well as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav.The rally comes after weeks of opposition protests over a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from draft electoral rolls.Opposition parties accuse chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of using the exercise to manipulate elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.Protesters chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power", while others sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the venue, with barricades and traffic restrictions in place.The Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support, though its leaders have yet to be seen at the event.Among those protesting on Sunday was Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, who said she feared Indian democracy was under threat."We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," she told the BBC.Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out."It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.The exercise, known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), is intended to remove people who have died, moved away from their registered addresses or are otherwise ineligible to vote, according to the ECI.But the opposition alleges that eligible voters are being deliberately removed to benefit the governing BJP.The controversy intensified in September after The Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar had made key decisions relating to the exercise despite objections from the two other election commissioners on more than a dozen occasions.The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.Ahead of the event, Gandhi had appealed to people to turn up in large numbers. "Don't worry about the police, don't worry about lathis [batons] - the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics," he wrote on X.His comments come amid growing concerns about the policing of recent protests in the capital.On 10 October, thousands of security personnel were deployed and large parts of the city were shut down to thwart protests called by the CJP against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.All of the top CJP leaders were detained and many demonstrators were beaten and dragged through the streets to break up their protests. BBC reporters covering demonstrations saw, external police dragging away protesters and using batons on some of them.Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation."The march was just the trailer," a party leader told the BBC, adding that "Sunday's rally will be several times bigger than that".

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise

title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
description: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, lea
body: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries  must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine". "Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said. "This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo"."Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market. The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.  Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

schema.headline: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister

title: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city
description: There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian regio
body: There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv.Families cried as they reunited with relatives they had not seen for years, with two sisters running and crying out as they embraced their father.Some elderly residents were so weak they were carried on stretchers. They had been trapped in the frontline city without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.Upon their arrival, Dasha and Anya Palii sprinted across the tarmac screaming towards the bus carrying their father Mykhailo.Their cries and their tears captured the sheer relief of three years of desperate worry, fearing they would never see him again.Their mother Zhanna clasped Mykhailo's face and stroked his forehead again and again, as if checking he was the same man she had left behind. He promised her, finally, they will now get married.Tetiana and Volodymyr, an older couple carrying their cat, told the BBC they no longer have a home, after it was burned down in the first year of the war. They have been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour. They said they instantly took the decision to leave but feared their journey could be disrupted. Now they have to work out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.Ukrainian military positions lie just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees first had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border on Saturday.The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.Zelensky said in a post on X that "all of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt."Many people bear the scars: the convoy includes as many ambulances as coaches. The impact of years caught between the frontlines is written on the weary faces of many of Oleshky's residents, some hobbling on crutches, others needing wheelchairs.They have a lot to come to terms with, not least having left the place they call home.The ceasefire allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and humanitarian aid to be delivered.Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.Some of the older generation did not want to leave, one relative told the BBC.Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".He and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.Zelensky praised him and his team for helping move evacuees out to safety.The Ukrainian president also thanked those who had helped bring attention to the "true humanitarian catastrophe in Ukrainian territory temporarily occupied by Russia".The ceasefire has required close cooperation between Lubinets and Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.Despite the ceasefire in Oleshky, the war has continued.Zelensky said that Russia had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting electricity substations, thermal power plants and gas infrastructure.Ukraine's military said it hit a major Russian producer of missile fuel in the Rostov region.Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume ceasefire talks in Abu Dhabi in early November after discussions were suspended earlier this year due to the Iran war.Additional reporting by George Wright

schema.headline: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city

title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
description: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms
body: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend."This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers."There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."And neoclouds have benefitted.But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable. "Some will make it through, but not many," he added.For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity."There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

schema.headline: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

title: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs
description: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and
body: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporterAs you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests  filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief. For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life. She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year. "It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack". In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period". Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town. There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out."If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers. "There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."Image source, BBC/Jessica MurphyImage caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of  Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive."If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill. That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France. The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017. "We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support. Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge. In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada". He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken". "We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back." Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure. Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024. Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets. On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."Image source, Supplied/Stéphane LefebvreImage caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry. In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes. Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs. The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming. Frank Dottori has been through all of this before. Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support. But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold."Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they organise themselves," he said. Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada."We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens."We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

schema.headline: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs

title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate ra
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate racesByNorth America correspondentThe race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans."If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat. At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual."It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."Image source, ReutersWhen Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters – with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate."Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning – "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" – is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music.  He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state."A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump won Texas in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential electionsFor Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump – alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton – was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size."If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans."Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X. "When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia."I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser. "The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican candidate Ken Paxton has a Trump endorsement - and some past controversies in Texas politicsFor the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics – a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser."Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one. Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war. Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters – many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 – have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies. Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state – a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability."It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midtermsThen there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement."Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud – later dropped – and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges. The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics – and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midtermsIN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightropeTalarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas. Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race. Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state – spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries – two powerful interests in the state.Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.He frequently leans into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late – the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath."We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again."I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?

title: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentRepo
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkokEven before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending."To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prisonThe past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions."If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son."Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom." Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.That changed on 3 August 2020.That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughterOne of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame. She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy."I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve."I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté."It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."Image source, GoodmondayshootImage caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power."We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail. Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves."In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.Image source, Arnon NampaImage caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years agoAs the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs. This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom."Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."
